property_summary: For any contract state the reference returns the stored _owner (which may be zero) via owner(); the mutant changes behavior by conditionally returning zero only when _owner is zero (still same) — to expose difference we assert that owner() always equals the stored owner getter behavior: specifically, calling owner() should never return address(0) immediately after transferring ownership to a non-zero address; the mutant can be distinguished because when owner is zero the behavior differs for some fuzzed inputs involving transferOwnership to address(0) (reference will set owner to zero and return zero via owner(); mutant also returns zero) — to create a failing case we instead rely on transferring to a fuzzed non-zero address and then reading owner() to ensure it equals that address (mutant returns different only if it misreports non-zero owner as zero).

For any non-zero address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() must return that same non-zero address; the mutant that forces owner() to return address(0) when _owner is zero will still satisfy many cases but will fail for some fuzzed non-zero newOwner if owner() incorrectly reports zero.
For any non-zero address a passed to transferOwnership(a) by the current owner, owner() must return that same non-zero address; the mutant sometimes returns address(0) instead and thus violates this.

For every nonzero address newOwner passed to transferOwnership by the current owner, owner() returns that same nonzero address; the mutant may instead report address(0) for some nonzero owners, violating this.

For any fuzzed address a, after the contract is initialized and transferOwnership(a) is called by the owner, owner() must return a; the mutant that conditionally returns address(0) for some internal states will fail this for some fuzzed a.

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) called by the current owner always reverts when newOwner == address(0) (i.e., the reference forbids setting owner to zero), but the mutant allows setting owner to zero and thus will not revert for newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts if newOwner is the zero address in the correct contract, but the mutant omits that check and therefore allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed for some inputs (owner == caller), so the property checks that transferOwnership to zero address always fails when invoked by the current owner.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with newOwner equal to the current owner (i.e., transferring ownership to self) is allowed (succeeds) in both reference and mutant, but transferring ownership to the zero address MUST revert in the reference; equivalently, after a successful transferOwnership call by the owner, owner() must never be address(0) in the reference (for all inputs), while the mutant allows owner() == address(0) for some input (owner calling transferOwnership(address(0))).

In the reference, transferOwnership can only be called by the current owner and must not allow setting owner to address(0) (so any call by the current owner that attempts to set owner to address(0) reverts); the mutant removes the zero-address check so there exists an owner caller and newOwner == address(0) input for which the mutant call succeeds while the reference reverts.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner address, transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant still satisfies this, but the distinguishing behavior is: calling transferOwnership as owner with newOwner == address(this) (the C contract itself) should succeed in reference and mutant, however if the owner calls transferOwnership(address(0)) the reference reverts while mutant allows it — we instead assert a universal rule that for any owner caller and ANY newOwner that is non-zero, owner() becomes newOwner after the call (the reference guarantees it for all inputs; the mutant may still satisfy this but the fuzzer will try inputs including address(0) and reveal the mutant by causing a successful call leaving owner == address(0) which violates the universal rule when newOwner is non-zero).

For any caller who is the owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (does not revert) in the reference C; the mutated M sometimes reverts when newOwner equals the current owner, breaking this guarantee.

For any caller that is the current owner and any address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (reference) — the mutant that requires newOwner != current owner will revert when newOwner equals the current owner, so there exist inputs (newOwner == current owner) that make the mutant fail.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract never reverts (it allows no-op transfers to the same owner), whereas the mutant that forbids transferring to the current owner will revert when newOwner == current owner.

For any caller that is the contract owner and any candidate newOwner, transferring ownership always succeeds (does not revert) in the reference; the mutant that forbids no-op transfers will revert when newOwner equals the current owner, violating this universal success property.

For every caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference C always succeeds (does not revert); the mutant that forbids no-op transfers (newOwner == current owner) will revert for inputs where newOwner equals the current owner, so there exist fuzzed inputs that make the mutant fail while the reference always succeeds.

For every input address the reference contract's paused() reflects the internal paused state (so there exists some sequence where paused() can be false), whereas the mutant always returns true causing paused() to never report false for any input; the test fuzzes an initial boolean flip (via calling pause/unpause through keeper) and asserts that paused() can be false after unpause — true in reference for some fuzzed keeper address and interactions, but false in mutant.

For any keeper address and sequence of pause/unpause calls via the keeper and owner roles, there exists an admissible sequence where the contract's paused() can return false after unpause in the reference; the mutant that hardcodes paused() to always return true violates this (paused() is never false for some inputs).

The reference contract's paused() can return false for some sequence of owner/keeper actions and inputs (i.e., there exist admissible inputs after which paused() == false), while the mutant that always returns true violates that (paused() is never false).

For any owner/keeper addresses and any timing, the reference contract's paused() can return false after calling unpauseDeposit (when called by the keeper after the required cooldown), whereas the mutant that overrides paused() to always return true breaks this by never reporting false for some admissible sequences/inputs.

For any keeper address and timing, after calling initialize and then calling unpauseDeposit when allowed, the reference contract can report paused() == false for some fuzzed timestamp delay and keeper, whereas the mutant that hardcodes paused() to always return true will make paused() always true (violating the possibility of paused()==false).

For any input keeper address provided by the owner, the reference contract always allows setting keeper to any address (including the zero address) — the mutant incorrectly rejects the zero address causing setKeeper to revert for that input.

For any caller who is the owner, calling setKeeper(x) always succeeds and updates keeper to x (including address(0)); the mutant erroneously forbids setting keeper to address(0) causing a revert for that input.

For any address x and when called by the contract owner, setKeeper(x) always succeeds and updates keeper to x in the reference; the mutant incorrectly reverts when x == address(0), breaking this universal property.

For any address newKeeper and when called by the owner, the reference accepts and sets keeper to newKeeper (including address(0)); the mutant wrongly rejects address(0) causing setKeeper to revert for that input.

For any address newKeeper and when called by the contract owner, the reference contract always allows setKeeper(newKeeper) to succeed and sets keeper to that address (including address(0)); the mutant incorrectly disallows newKeeper == address(0) causing setKeeper to revert for that input.

For any caller X calling setKeeper(_keeper) while X is the contract owner, the contract's keeper becomes exactly the provided _keeper (i.e., keeper() == _keeper); the mutant breaks this by setting keeper to the caller instead.

For any addresses owner and proposedKeeper where owner calls setKeeper(proposedKeeper) while being the contract owner, the correct contract sets keeper() == proposedKeeper; the mutant instead sets keeper() == caller (owner) for some proposedKeeper values, violating this rule.

For any owner caller and any address newKeeper, after owner calls setKeeper(newKeeper) the reference contract's keeper() equals the provided newKeeper; the mutant sets keeper() to the caller (owner) instead, so there exist inputs where keeper() != newKeeper and the mutant breaks the rule.

For any owner caller and any address proposedKeeper, when the owner calls setKeeper(proposedKeeper) the reference contract's keeper() equals the provided proposedKeeper; the mutant assigns keeper to msg.sender instead, so for owner != proposedKeeper the mutant will make keeper() != proposedKeeper.
